# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are both communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Slack who are considering switching to Element, possibly due to concerns over data ownership or cost. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Element allows teams to retain full ownership of their data, while Slack's data ownership policies are more restrictive.
* Setup Complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack has better scalability for very large teams, while Element can be more challenging to scale.
* Integration with Video Conferencing: Slack has native integration with Zoom, while Element has integration with Jitsi for video conferencing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Robust support resources
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Full data ownership and control
* End-to-end encryption for security
* Customizable and extensible
* Open-source and community-driven
However, Element's limitations include:
* Steeper learning curve for self-hosting
* Limited support resources compared to Slack
* Fewer integrations with third-party tools
* Less polished user interface
* Limited scalability for very large teams

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Slack: Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use, have a large budget, and require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools. It's also a good choice for teams that don't have the technical expertise to self-host a communication platform. Slack is well-suited for large teams with complex communication needs.
When to choose Element: Element is a good choice for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, have a limited budget, and are comfortable with self-hosting a communication platform. It's also a good choice for teams that require end-to-end encryption for security. Element is well-suited for small to medium-sized teams with simple communication needs.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which exports data in JSON format.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with third-party tools.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and features of Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability can be challenging for very large teams. However, for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching if you have a small to medium-sized team with simple communication needs and are comfortable with self-hosting.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need a wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and control
* Teams that require end-to-end encryption for security
* Teams with technical expertise that can self-host a communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any per-user costs.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve than Slack, especially for self-hosting.
### Can I integrate Element with third-party tools?
Yes, Element has some integrations with third-party tools, but not as many as Slack.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption for security, which means your data is protected from interception.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those valuing data ownership and customization. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch is to gain control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to support large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives teams more control over their infrastructure.
* Integration: Mattermost has a more extensive library of custom integrations, including support for GitLab and Jenkins, while Slack has a wider range of pre-built integrations with popular services.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of pre-built integrations
* Strong mobile app support
* Large user community
* Regularly updated with new features
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for data control and customization
* Customizable and extensible through integrations and plugins
* Free, open-source option
* Strong support for developer teams
* Limitations in mobile app support and ease of use for non-technical users

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of pre-built integrations. It's ideal for small to medium-sized teams that don't require a high level of customization or data control. On the other hand, Mattermost is suited for teams that value data ownership and customization, such as large enterprises or developer teams. It's also a good choice for teams with complex integration requirements or those that need to comply with strict data regulations.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance, including setting up integrations and customizing your workflow.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure that all features are working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is production-ready for most users, offering a stable and feature-rich platform for team collaboration. However, one technical limitation to consider is Mattermost's limited support for mobile apps, which can make it less convenient for teams that rely heavily on mobile devices. Based on our analysis, we recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a team that values data ownership and customization, and doesn't require a high level of mobile app support.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need mobile app support and want to reduce costs.
* Developer teams that require custom integrations and a high level of data control.
* Large enterprises that need to comply with strict data regulations and want to self-host their communication platform.
* Teams that don't require a wide range of pre-built integrations and want to customize their workflow.
* Teams with complex integration requirements that can be met through Mattermost's custom integrations and plugins.

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, giving teams full control over their data and customization.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free and open-source, with a self-hosted option available at no cost.
### Does Mattermost support mobile apps?
Mattermost has limited support for mobile apps, with some features not available on mobile devices.
### Can I import my Slack data into Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers an import tool that supports importing data from Slack, including channels, users, and messages.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Yes, Mattermost is suitable for small teams, offering a free, self-hosted option and customizable features.

title: Discord vs Element
comparison_markdown:
# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Element is a free, self-hosted alternative to Discord. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control systems that help developers manage and collaborate on code. This comparison is beneficial for development teams, especially those considering switching from GitHub to GitLab for more control over their data and costs. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and autonomy over their development workflow.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free plans with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted version with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up and use, especially for small teams, while GitLab requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: GitLab is more scalable than GitHub, especially for large teams and enterprises.
* Integration: GitLab has a built-in continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) feature, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations for CI/CD.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Free plan available
* Limited control over data and workflow
**GitLab:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD features
* Highly scalable
* Free self-hosted version available
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data and workflow. It's also a good choice for teams already invested in the GitHub ecosystem. GitLab, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams and enterprises that require more control over their data, workflow, and scalability. It's also a good choice for teams that want to self-host their repositories and have built-in CI/CD features.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub API or the `git archive` command.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and import your exported repository using the GitLab import tool.
3. Update your local repository to point to the new GitLab repository using the `git remote` command.
4. Verify that all your data, including issues and pull requests, has been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
GitLab is production-ready for most users, offering a robust and feature-rich platform for version control and collaboration. However, one technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted version requires significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. For teams that require full control over their data and workflow, GitLab is a clear winner, while smaller teams that prioritize ease of use may want to stick with GitHub.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that require full control over their data and workflow
* Large enterprises that need scalable version control and CI/CD features
* Teams that want to self-host their repositories and have built-in CI/CD features
* Developers who don't need GitHub's large community and ecosystem
* Teams with fewer than 10 users that don't need GitHub's free plan features

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted version with most features.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab as easy to use as GitHub?
No, GitLab has a steeper learning curve and more complex setup.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository and import it into GitLab.
### Does GitLab have built-in CI/CD features?
Yes, GitLab has built-in CI/CD features, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by individuals and teams to create user interfaces, websites, and applications. This comparison is beneficial for designers, developers, and product managers who are looking for a cost-effective and flexible solution. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design, and the key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma has a per-user pricing model, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Figma stores data on its servers, while Penpot allows self-hosting for full data control.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Feature difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of features, including advanced prototyping and collaboration tools, while Penpot has a more limited feature set but is rapidly developing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Figma Pros:**
* Comprehensive set of features
* Large community and ecosystem
* Well-established and reliable
* Advanced collaboration tools
* Scalable for large teams
**Figma Cons:**
* Expensive for large teams
* Limited control over data
* Proprietary license
* Limited customization options
**Penpot Pros:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for data control
* Rapidly developing feature set
* Customizable and extensible
* Cost-effective for small teams
**Penpot Cons:**
* Limited features compared to Figma
* Technical expertise required for self-hosting
* Smaller community and ecosystem
* Still in development, with some bugs and instability
* Limited support for advanced prototyping

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a comprehensive set of features, advanced collaboration tools, and scalability. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay a premium for a well-established and reliable solution. On the other hand, Penpot is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, or organizations that prioritize cost-effectiveness, data control, and customization. It is also suitable for teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and have the technical expertise to manage their own infrastructure.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to import your designs into Penpot.
3. Review and adjust your designs to take advantage of Penpot's features and customization options.
4. Set up your Penpot instance, either self-hosted or using the cloud service.
5. Invite your team to collaborate on your designs in Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in the early stages of development, and while it shows promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's performance can be slow with large and complex designs. However, for small teams or individuals who prioritize cost-effectiveness and data control, Penpot is definitely worth considering, and we recommend switching from Figma if you don't need advanced features like prototyping or a large community.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need advanced features
* Individuals who prioritize cost-effectiveness and data control
* Organizations with limited budgets that still need a collaborative design tool
* Teams that require self-hosting for data control and customization
* Developers who want to extend and customize their design tool

## FAQ
### Is Penpot free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, with no per-user costs.
### Can I self-host Penpot?

### Is Penpot compatible with Figma files?
Yes, Penpot can import Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.

No, Penpot's community is still small compared to Figma's.

Not yet, Penpot is still in development and may not be scalable for large teams.
